extracted.intended_audience: Section 1557 covered entities (health care providers, health plans, and other entities using patient care decision support tools)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory requirements under §92.210 implementing Section 1557 nondiscrimination obligations for covered entities that use patient care decision support tools (including predictive DSIs and non-automated evidence-based tools) in clinical decision-making. Covers definitions, identification and mitigation obligations, enforcement factors, examples, and interaction with other agencies' rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'patient care decision support tool'
rubrics_metrics.description: §92.210 defines 'patient care decision support tool' to include tools used to support clinical decision-making that derive outputs (prediction, classification, recommendation, evaluation, or analysis) from algorithms or models (Predictive DSIs) and also includes non-automated, evidence-based tools that rely on rules, assumptions, constraints, or thresholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include predictive decision support interventions (as defined by ONC), flowcharts (e.g., Crisis Standards of Care), formulas, equations, calculators, algorithms, utilization management applications, software as medical devices (SaMDs), software in medical devices (SiMDs), screening, risk assessment and eligibility tools, and diagnostic and treatment guidance tools. The definition covers autonomous tools and tools that assist or augment clinical decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: applies only to clinical decision-making in covered entity programs/activities
rubrics_metrics.description: §92.210 applies to patient care decision support tools used in a covered entity's health programs or activities to support clinical decision-making affecting patient care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provision does not apply to tools unrelated to clinical decision-making (when they are unrelated to health programs/activities), such as administrative/billing activities, automated medical coding, fraud/waste/abuse detection, patient scheduling, facilities or inventory management, supply chain, financial investment management, or employment and staffing-related activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: General prohibition on discrimination via decision support tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered entities are prohibited from discriminating on the basis of race, color, national origin, sex, age, or disability in their health programs or activities through the use of patient care decision support tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central substantive prohibition that §92.210 operationalizes for uses of clinical algorithms and other decision support tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to make reasonable efforts to identify tools with protected-basis inputs (§92.210(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered entities must make reasonable efforts to identify patient care decision support tools used in their health programs or activities that employ input variables or factors that measure race, color, national origin, sex, age, or disability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covered entities are not required to identify all tools that indirectly measure protected characteristics, given the many possible indirect measures, but should exercise caution for tools known to use indirect measures. Entities need not obtain developers' datasets by default; however, if they have reason to believe a tool uses such variables or otherwise know or should know it could result in discrimination, they should consult publicly available sources or request information from the developer. ONC-certified Health IT disclosures may assist covered entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to make reasonable efforts to mitigate discrimination (§92.210(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: For each patient care decision support tool identified under §92.210(b), covered entities must make reasonable efforts to mitigate the risk of discrimination resulting from the tool's use in their health programs or activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule sets a 'reasonable efforts' mitigation standard rather than prescribing specific mitigation techniques. Examples of mitigation include discontinuing use of a discriminatory input (e.g., stop using a race-adjusted eGFR and use a revised non-race equation) and implementing staff protocols to ensure proper use. OCR will evaluate mitigation measures on a case-by-case basis. Covered entities may adopt more robust safeguards as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable efforts is context-dependent and flexible
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'reasonable efforts' standard allows variation in the extent of identification and mitigation obligations based on the covered entity's circumstances and the characteristics of the input variable or tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR notes factors such as the relative suspectness of an input (e.g., race merits greater scrutiny than age) and that age inputs may be clinically indicated and need less mitigation if supported by evidence-based clinical practice. The Age Act allows some age distinctions in specified contexts. The reasonable efforts requirement balances mitigation needs with burdens on covered entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: OCR enforcement will be fact-specific; assessment factors for 'reasonable efforts to identify'
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR will assess compliance with §92.210(b) and (c) on a case-by-case basis and may consider specific factors when evaluating whether a covered entity made reasonable efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR may consider (1) covered entity size and resources (larger entities expected to do more), (2) whether the tool was used as intended or was adapted/customized, (3) whether the entity received product information from the developer about potential for discrimination or identified that the tool's inputs include protected bases, and (4) whether the entity has a methodology/process (e.g., seeking developer information, reviewing medical literature, membership association inputs, analyzing complaints) for evaluating adopted tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proxy discrimination is prohibited and merits caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1557 prohibits proxy discrimination — the use of variables that function as indirect measures of protected bases — and this principle applies to §92.210.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given many possible indirect measures of race, color, national origin, sex, age, and disability, covered entities are not required to identify all indirect measures but should exercise caution when tools are known to use proxies for protected characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covered entities' knowledge and information-gathering duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered entities may not be required to obtain developers' training datasets, but if they know or have reason to believe a tool uses variables measuring protected bases, they should consult public sources or request information from the developer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ONC's rule requires some disclosures by developers of certified Health IT that will help covered entities learn about source attributes and risk management practices. Covered entities subject to HIPAA may obtain documentation of a tool's use in an individual's medical record via the HIPAA right of access when recorded in the designated record set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency requirements not imposed by §92.210 (but voluntary disclosure recommended)
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR declines to require covered entities to notify patients about the patient care decision support tools used in their health programs or to disclose training data, assumptions, constraints, thresholds, or other inputs as a regulatory mandate under §92.210.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR notes costs and practical barriers (developer non-disclosure, frequent tool changes). It nevertheless calls voluntary disclosure a best practice but cautions that voluntary disclosure alone does not ensure compliance with §92.210. Other agencies or future guidance may impose transparency requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with other regulatory frameworks (ONC, FDA, NIST)
rubrics_metrics.description: §92.210 is not duplicative of ONC's Predictive DSI rule (which applies to developers); §92.210 applies to covered entity users. FDA regulates devices and may limit bias premarket but post-market deployment can still introduce discriminatory bias. NIST AI RMF is consistent with mitigation approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR will coordinate with FDA, ONC, and other Federal partners to ensure consistency. Covered entities should be aware of ONC and FDA requirements and use ONC-certified Health IT disclosures and FDA communications as information sources when evaluating tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: No strict liability imposed on covered entities; developers and entities have independent obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR declines to impose strict liability on covered entities for discriminatory outcomes of tools or to create a developer-safe-harbor that relieves covered entities of obligation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each covered entity is independently required to comply with Section 1557 including §92.210; a covered provider's liability under Section 1557 is not contingent on a developer's liability. OCR declines to impose strict liability on covered entities or developers in this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources and examples that may indicate discriminatory risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered entities may learn that a tool poses discriminatory risk through peer-reviewed medical journals, FDA safety communications, Agency reports (e.g., AHRQ), media reporting of reliable studies, professional and hospital associations, health insurance associations, nonprofit AI organizations, and ONC disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR cited examples such as the race-adjusted eGFR equation, Crisis Standards of Care triage flowcharts, medical necessity review tools denying rehabilitative care, and pulse oximeter racial discrepancies as instances where research or advisories revealed discriminatory impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouraged mitigation best practices (non-prescriptive)
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR identifies several mitigation techniques as best practices that covered entities may adopt to reduce discriminatory risk but does not require specific measures under §92.210(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested best practices include developing and implementing policies specific to algorithm use, establishing governance measures, monitoring impacts, addressing complaints, staff training on proper use, using tools consistent with FDA clearance and developer intended uses, using peer-reviewed research to inform adjustments, requesting assessments from developers, and documenting mitigation efforts for OCR review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-by-case remediation and technical assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR will investigate complaints with fact-specific analyses and may provide technical assistance and engage stakeholders to revise discriminatory guidelines or tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past OCR investigations (e.g., State Crisis Standards of Care) included extensive technical assistance and resulted in revisions to remove alleged discriminatory provisions. OCR may provide guidance or future rulemaking and will consider additional actions to support covered entities consistent with Federal law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for compliance: delayed applicability to allow implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: The final §92.210 includes a delayed applicability date of no later than 300 days after the final rule's effective date to give covered entities a reasonable period to come into compliance with §92.210(b) and (c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a procedural accommodation acknowledging implementation burdens and the need for coordination with other agencies and stakeholders.
